notes.claim: The adiabatic check ensures the protective conductor can withstand the energy let-through of the device under earth fault conditions: S = √(I²t) / k, with k depending on conductor material, insulation and temperatures.
The slides take k from Tables 54.2 to 54.6 and, for the 1.5 mm² cpc, S = √(341.4² × 0.1) / 115 = 0.93 mm², and with Cmax at 395.3 A, 1.08 mm².
Cmax is advised when determining the fault current carrying capacity of conductors and Cmin for the current that operates the device.
The adiabatic equation is only valid for disconnection times not exceeding 5 seconds, and I²t is the energy let-through in A²s.
The live conductors must also withstand short circuit current: the slides find the minimum fault at Cmin (177.6 A), the maximum at Cmax (205.6 A), and t = k²S²/I² = 3.02 s for k = 143 and 2.5 mm².
IPF is whichever is highest of PEFC and PSCC, and the device's breaking capacity Icn must exceed it (IPF ≤ Icn) or the device may destroy itself in a short circuit or earth fault.
The project guide allows the SWA to be used as the cpc if justified by calculation, and flowchart note 2 separates a suitable cpc size from the minimum cpc size.

A cable's armour may serve as the cpc where it is justified by calculation (the project guide); the calculation is the adiabatic equation on the armour's steel area, and the armour's resistance goes into Zs = Ze + (R1+R2) like any other conductor.

The k for a 90 °C thermosetting copper conductor is 143 (Table 43.1, also a copper cpc in the cable); for steel armour of an XLPE cable one trade calculator lists 46, far below copper, so the armour must have the larger area; the k depends on the starting temperature, so a cpc in the cable (Table 54.3) differs from a separate one (Table 54.2); read Table 54.4 in your own copy.

A maker states the armour of a four-core XLPE/SWA/PVC cable in mm² and Ω/km at 20 °C by core size (for the 4 mm² cable 22 mm² and 6.8 Ω/km; 1.5 mm²: 17 mm², 8.8 Ω/km; 2.5 mm²: 20 mm², 7.7 Ω/km; 6 mm²: 36 mm², 4.3 Ω/km; 10 mm²: 42 mm², 3.7 Ω/km), and an armour short-circuit rating for 1 s (1.0 kA for the 4 mm² four-core).
The armour runs about 10 °C cooler than the cores at full load, so a resistance worked at the cores' temperature is cautious; the maker's ratings are adiabatic.

For a short circuit the live conductors must take the let-through energy (Reg 434.5.2): the time to reach the limiting temperature is t = k²S² ÷ I², and the cable's energy withstand must be at least the device's let-through; I at Cmax and the time from the device.
A circuit-breaker's let-through energy I²t is limited by its energy-limiting class; a type C breaker opens in under 0.1 s at 10 In or more.

Prospective fault current is determined at every relevant point (Reg 434.1) and every device's rated short-circuit breaking capacity must not be less than it where the device is installed (Reg 434.5.1); a lower rating is allowed only if a device on the supply side has the necessary rating; above its Icn a breaker may fail to clear the fault and destroy the board.
The maker declares Icn; BS EN 60898 standard values run from 1 500 A to 25 000 A and include 4 500 A, 6 000 A and 10 000 A; MCBs are commonly marked 6 kA or 10 kA.

The 4.6 kA in the assignment is about twice 230 V ÷ 0.1 Ω = 2 300 A: on a three-phase supply the highest prospective fault current is the simultaneous three-phase fault, approximated from the line-neutral reading multiplied by 2, because the line-neutral loop is one line plus one return while in the three-phase fault the return carries nothing; some call the doubling a rule of thumb that overstates, and a line-to-line reading divided by 0.87 is the closer method.

The formula sheet gives step 18/19 as S = √I²t ÷ k; C&G papers ask for the cpc's thermal constraints under fault conditions and for the live conductors' adequacy in a short circuit to Reg 434.5.2, and for a short-circuit check on a small cable.
